overview: Jamaica’s history is full of skilled makers and memorable voices. A carved wooden spirit figure, a kitchen recovered from the sea and locally made clay pots offer different windows into the past. Maroon traditions, Miss Lou’s performances and reggae show people creating, preserving and sharing knowledge across generations.

periods.title: Taíno carving traditions
periods.summary: Surviving wooden figures preserve evidence of Indigenous craftsmanship and spiritual life. This selected phase is not a date for Jamaica’s first inhabitants.

periods.title: European contact
periods.summary: Columbus reached Jamaica in 1494. Spanish colonisation followed; the island already had Indigenous communities.

periods.title: Spanish colonial rule
periods.summary: Spanish colonists established Sevilla la Nueva in 1509. Spanish Town later became the colonial government centre.

periods.title: English and British plantation colony
periods.summary: English forces captured Jamaica in 1655. Plantation sugar production expanded through the forced labour of enslaved Africans, alongside resistance and Maroon communities.

periods.title: Apprenticeship after abolition
periods.summary: The 1834 emancipation settlement imposed apprenticeship before full emancipation in 1838.

periods.title: Emancipation under colonial rule
periods.summary: Full emancipation ended apprenticeship in 1838. British colonial government and unequal political power continued.

periods.title: Broader voting rights and independence movement
periods.summary: The first general election under universal adult suffrage took place in December 1944. Jamaica remained a colony during its subsequent constitutional changes.

periods.title: Independent Jamaica
periods.summary: Jamaica became independent on August 6, 1962. Its elected government took responsibility for national affairs.

sections.title: Discoveries: wood, clay and a sunken kitchen

items.text: A Taíno wooden figure known as the Birdman was reported found in a Jamaican cave in 1792. Its beak and wings combine bird and human features, with surviving shell inlay. Scientific study places its wood around 1000 to 1150 CE. Carved from hard guaiacum, it preserves extraordinary woodworking skill, although its precise original ritual setting is unknown.

In Port Royal’s submerged Building 4, archaeologists found iron cooking pots, copper pails, a wooden bucket, pewter spoons and ceramic bowls on a brick kitchen floor. These objects survived the city’s 1692 earthquake. Together they reveal equipment for preparing and serving food; they do not identify the cooks or tell us exactly what was on the menu.

Excavations at New Street in Port Royal recovered fragments of locally made cooking and storage vessels from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. DAACS researchers compare clay, firing traces and shaping marks to distinguish different ways of making pottery. Enslaved Jamaicans produced and traded these wares: the objects record craft and exchange within a system that denied their makers freedom.

A small handmade clay whistle also came from the New Street excavations. Researchers think it was probably made in eighteenth-century Jamaica by an enslaved person. Its maker and user remain unidentified. We can recognise an object designed to make sound without deciding that it was definitely a child’s toy or inventing the tune someone played.

sections.title: Home life, including the toilet question

items.text: Late seventeenth-century Port Royal inventories describe parlors used for both entertaining and sleeping. Some beds could fold away during the day. A room might have to be ready for visitors after being somebody’s bedroom. These lists record possessions after property owners died, so they show particular households rather than how every Jamaican lived.

One Port Royal parlor inventory includes a “close stoole chaire”: a toilet chair of a type that held a chamber pot beneath the seat. Furniture could have a surprisingly practical second job. The inventory records the chair, but says nothing about who emptied its pot. That missing task matters when imagining the household’s daily work.

At Moore Town in eastern Jamaica, Maroon heritage includes the abeng, a horn blown through an opening in its side and used for communication over distance. Descendants of communities that escaped enslavement preserve this knowledge alongside their own institutions and communally held land. Passing on a tradition can mean learning how to listen as well as how to make a sound.

Moore Town’s Kromanti ceremonies bring together singing, dancing and distinctive drumming to invoke ancestral spirits. They draw on African traditions reshaped within the Maroon community. These are religious practices with meaning for participants, not simply a stage performance. UNESCO also records missionary opposition and migration as pressures on their transmission.

As a girl in early nineteenth-century Kingston, Mary Seacole learned to care for patients by watching her mother at work. Her mother ran a lodging house where army officers and their families also received care. Seacole later helped with patients herself. In this household, learning a caring profession began through observation and participation, before her better-known work overseas.

Louise Bennett-Coverley, known as Miss Lou, welcomed children into stories, folk songs, dance and poetry through her television programme Ring Ding. She championed Jamaican Creole as a language worthy of performance and literature. Children could hear familiar speech celebrated in public and participate in cultural life themselves. Their voices belonged in the show.

Reggae grew from Jamaican musical creativity, especially in Western Kingston, drawing on earlier local styles and sounds circulating around the Caribbean and beyond. Its songs could address injustice and resistance as well as love and spiritual life. Listening to music can therefore open a conversation about society, not just provide a beat for dancing.

In a 2017 letter, Edna Manley College described courses exploring reggae’s history and development, alongside a folk collection assembled by Olive Lewin. The college’s arts schools had come together in 1976. Learning about music could involve both performing it and studying how earlier generations made it: instruments and archives both had a place.

Jamaica became independent on August 6, 1962, with Alexander Bustamante as its first prime minister. Responsibility shifted from British colonial control to Jamaica’s elected government. The change concerned who governed the country; its people’s languages, family knowledge and cultural creativity had histories reaching far beyond that constitutional date.

ending.text: British colonial rule ended with independence in 1962. Jamaica continues as an independent country, while communities sustain and reshape their own cultural traditions. Political independence is a change in sovereignty, not the beginning or ending of the island’s people.
